title: Segmentation patterns and failover for serving modes
content:
Purpose

This is a working note to compare practical segmentation (isolation) patterns and failover strategies across the three serving modes we operate: Hosted, Dedicated, Private. The goal is to produce an operational checklist and a small decision matrix we can use when designing tenant routing for a new workload or rollout.

Audience and context
- Platform engineers who own routing, capacity, and control-plane policies.
- Solutions engineers advising customers on deployment choices.
- SRE/observability owners for metrics and runbooks.

High-level summary (one-liners)
- Hosted: multi-tenant compute + shared control plane; strong logical isolation, soft physical isolation; routing emphasizes cost/latency optimization and autoscaling policies.
- Dedicated: tenant-reserved pools; physical/compute isolation; control plane typically still shared (control-plane tenancy) or logically partitioned; routing focuses on capacity guarantees and predictable SLOs.
- Private: tenant-managed control plane or private control-plane + private compute; full isolation (network + data); routing is customer-local (VPC/on-prem) with limited platform-level steering.

Key isolation boundary axes (how we should think about them)
- Network boundary: private VPC vs shared network with ACLs/segmentation.
- Compute boundary: dedicated GPU pools vs multiplexed hosts.
- Control plane boundary: shared SaaS control plane vs tenant-specific control plane instance.
- Data plane & telemetry: whether logs/metrics traverse platform telemetry or stay in customer account.
- Metadata/Config: who stores routing policy, allowed model versions, rollout configs.

Decision matrix (text table)
- Rows: Isolation axis listed above. Columns: Hosted / Dedicated / Private. Short notes below each cell.
Hosted:
  Network: shared VPC overlay, per-tenant NS/SG rules (soft isolation)
  Compute: GPU multiplexing, dynamic packing, tenant co-location by affinity policies
  Control plane: single global control plane (multi-tenant RBAC)
  Telemetry: platform-first telemetry (customer-level partitions)
  Config: central repo, per-tenant scopes
Dedicated:
  Network: optional L3 isolation or customer-dedicated subnets in cloud region
  Compute: reserved pools, pinned instance types, no noisy neighbors guarantees
  Control plane: shared control plane but per-tenant config/namespace; optional private control-plane addon
  Telemetry: split — platform collects, customer can opt-in to forward to own sinks
  Config: per-reservation policies (capacity, burst rules)
Private:
  Network: customer-controlled VPC/on-prem with private routing
  Compute: fully customer-owned or dedicated hardware in customer project
  Control plane: tenant-run control plane or customer-managed control plane instance
  Telemetry: remains in customer domain, platform has reduced access (audit-only)
  Config: customer stores routing and rollouts locally

Routing decision points (where routing can happen)
- Public ingress/edge: earliest decision point. Best for geo-routing, rate-limiting and quick model variant selection based on global policies.
- Control-plane routing service: authoritative policy engine for tenant-level routing decisions, version pinning, and circuit-breakers.
- Local agent / node router: last-mile decisions (hot failover to local cache, KV prefix reuse, local capacity checks).

Recommended placement of routing logic per mode
- Hosted: keep policy in central control plane (fast reads + fallback caches at edge). Edge should be read-through cache for control-plane decisions to reduce RTT.
- Dedicated: control-plane remains authoritative but allow per-reservation overrides stored with the reservation metadata. Edge caches must honor reservation-level knobs (no cross-tenant oversubscribe).
- Private: prefer local control-plane or config that is authoritative. Platform-level routing decisions should only be advisory unless customer elects centralized management.

Failure modes and guarded fallback strategies (operational)
1) Control-plane unavailable (partitioned from data plane)
   - Hosted: edge caches used for up to X minutes (configurable TTL). Fallback: route to compatible model family/cheaper quantized variant; degrade streaming to chunked responses.
   - Dedicated: failover to prewired burst accounts or move to regional failover pool attached to reservation (if configured). If reservation strict, reject new requests with explicit 503 + retry-after.
   - Private: keep local agent as authoritative; if control-plane is remote and unreachable, fail closed if customer policy requires—otherwise local fallback.
2) Capacity exhaustion (hot spots)
   - Soft capacity: use routing policies to shift low-priority tenants to cheaper region/variant. Prioritize by SLA tier + queued request TTL.
   - Hard capacity on Dedicated: honor reservation; if reservation saturated, use burst credit if enabled or surface backpressure to the client.
3) Region outage
   - Use geo-aware routing at edge to redirect to next closest region with pinned model variants. For Private with on-prem, regional failover is a customer decision; platform can propose templates.

Example request routing flow (edge -> control -> node)
- Client -> CDN/edge ingress (auth verification)
- Edge consults local routing cache: has mapping (tenant->reservation->region->model_variant)? yes -> forward to assigned region endpoint.
- If cache miss -> edge calls control-plane policy service with tenant id and request metadata.
- Control-plane returns route, SLO class, and fallback hints (model fallback order, burst account id).
- Edge persists cache entry (TTL small: 30s–2m depending on churn).
- Target region node validates reservation and either accepts or tells edge to fallback.

Sequence diagram (compact ASCII)
Client -> Edge: request + tenant_id
Edge -> ControlPlane: getRoute(tenant_id) [if miss]
ControlPlane -> Edge: route{region, pool, model, fallbackList}
Edge -> Node(pool): forward(req)
Node -> Edge: accept | full -> (fallback)
Edge -> Node(alt): forward(req)

Operational knobs we must expose to customers (recommended)
- Reservation capacity and burst credit settings (Dedicated)
- Allowed fallback model families and quality tiers
- Region pinning / geo-preference
- Local cache TTL for routing decisions
- Emergency fail-open vs fail-closed preference

Implementation checklist (actionable items)
- [ ] Define canonical routing cache schema (fields: tenant_id, reservation_id, region, pool_id, allowed_variants, fallback_list, ttl)
- [ ] Edge: implement cache with tombstones and fast invalidation hooks
- [ ] Control-plane: add per-tenant allocation API returning route + metric tags + fallback hints
- [ ] Dedicated: reservation metadata API (burst credits + autoscale constraints)
- [ ] Private: design "agent-sync" protocol for local authoritative routing + audit interface
- [ ] Test harness: simulate control-plane outage + capacity spikes for all three modes
- [ ] Update runbooks with specific 503/429 semantics per mode

Open questions / unresolved tradeoffs
- How long is "safe" for edge cache TTL in Hosted for consistency vs cost of control plane calls? (suggested experiments: 15s/60s/180s for synthesized traffic)
- For Dedicated, should we allow cross-reservation emergency borrowing in extreme scenarios or never? (billing/SLAs implication)
- For Private mode, what minimum telemetry must platform retain for security incident investigation without violating isolation?
- Do customers prefer a single control-plane endpoint with RBAC for Private (managed) or a fully air-gapped option only?

Notes from recent incident (postmortem sketch)
- Incident: control-plane throttling event -> hosted edge caches expired -> 80% of traffic experienced control-plane lookup latencies -> cascading retries -> increased tail latencies and dropped streaming connections.
- Short term mitigation: increase edge cache TTL and add circuit-breaker on lookup path.
- Long term: implement token-bucket for control-plane lookup rate and prefetching heuristics for tenants with recent traffic.

Conclusions and next steps
- For productization: publish a small "routing expectations" one-pager for each mode summarizing SLO, failover behavior, and customer opt-in knobs.
- Prioritize building the canonical cache schema + control-plane allocation API as these are low-effort/high-impact.
- Run chaos tests for control-plane partition scenarios against Hosted and Dedicated to measure tolerable cache TTL values.

Quick links and references
- Related platform design notes: CONFLUENCE-PLAT-456 (linked_artifacts)
- Incident ticket: JIRA-ENG-2318
- Prototype agent sync RFC: github PR (linked_artifacts)

-- end of working note --

Notes to self: keep this doc lightweight. Convert to a formal playbook after we validate TTL experiments and prototype the control-plane allocation API.
